summary: Cape Florida Light on Key Biscayne: lit 1825, burned by Seminoles in 1836, rebuilt, dark 1878-1978, now a state park with tower tours.

structures.note: first tower, 65 ft (20 m); damaged by fire in the 1836 Seminole attack (nomination; LighthouseFriends)
second tower, completed 1846; raised from 65 ft to 95 ft (29 m) in 1855 (nomination; Rowlett)

access.note: Bill Baggs Cape Florida State Park; tower tours on select days (VisitFlorida).

facts.agency: State of Florida (Bill Baggs Cape Florida State Park)

events.note: Congress appropriates $8,000 for a light on Cape Florida (LighthouseFriends)
Contract awarded to Samuel B. Lincoln of Boston (LighthouseFriends); the nomination names Samuel Lincoln as the contractor
Brick tower of 65 ft (20 m) completed by the end of 1825; the nomination says Noah Humphreys certified it on 1 December 1825
Lit 17 December 1825 (LighthouseFriends); the Society's record gives 1825 as the year established
John Dubose appointed first keeper
Seminole attack on 23 July 1836 sets the tower and keeper's house afire
Second Seminole War attack; assistant keeper John W. B. Thompson survives; helper Aaron Carter killed (LighthouseFriends)
Boats from the schooner Motto and the sloop-of-war Concord reach Thompson the next morning; he is hauled down by line
Congress appropriates $10,000 to rebuild (LighthouseFriends); rebuilding authorized in 1837 (nomination)
Second tower completed; the nomination says 1846, LighthouseFriends says a $13,000 appropriation of 10 August 1846 and a finish in 1847
Tower raised from 65 ft to 95 ft (nomination; Rowlett)
New second-order Fresnel lens on Lieutenant George G. Meade's recommendation (LighthouseFriends)
Lamp removed and lens prisms smashed in August 1861 by a trio of southern sympathizers (LighthouseFriends); the nomination says 'a band of lawless persons'
Back in service 15 April 1866 (LighthouseFriends); the nomination says not back in operation until 1867
Extinguished 15 June 1878 when the Fowey Rocks light went into operation
Light-House Board report: a tender assisted in a survey of the old Cape Florida Reservation
State of Florida purchases the lighthouse and the tip of Key Biscayne (LighthouseFriends)
Bill Baggs Cape Florida State Park opens in January 1967 (LighthouseFriends)
Replica keeper's house and station buildings built (Rowlett; USLHS record); LighthouseFriends dates the rebuilding to 1978
Relit 4 July 1978 (LighthouseFriends); Rowlett lists it as reactivated 1978
Hurricane Andrew damages the tower in August 1992; the light is out until restoration (LighthouseFriends)
Tower restored in time for Miami's centennial (LighthouseFriends); Rowlett lists a 300 mm lens in 1996

notes_for_editor: Conflicts left open in the story: (1) rebuilding finish, 1846 (nomination; Rowlett) against 1847 (LighthouseFriends); (2) the Civil War repair, 15 April 1866 (LighthouseFriends) against 1867 (nomination); (3) the 1864 'rebuilt' date in the nomination's introduction conflicts with its own 1846 and is not used; (4) Lincoln's fate: LighthouseFriends says he was lost at sea, the nomination says he built the tower and Humphreys certified it; (5) lamps, 15 or 17; (6) replica station buildings, 1970 (Rowlett; Society) or 1978 (LighthouseFriends); (7) the dark years after 1978, 1990-1996 (Rowlett) or the 1992 hurricane (LighthouseFriends). The NRHP nomination is OCR'd: quotes were chosen where the OCR is clean; a few words are reconstructed from context. Thompson's letter appears in two prints (Richmond Palladium 26 Nov 1836; AccessGenealogy); the Richmond print's OCR is poor, so quotes are taken from AccessGenealogy and checked against both. The letter dates the rescue 'Monday, July 5th' (sic); the story does not use that date. The Light-House Board 1901 entry (scan p. 184) is a tender paragraph; the tender's name and the printed page number were not read and the citation is by scan page. Roster matched by name; the Society's position is 7.3 km from the station record's. LighthouseFriends is a copyrighted site: facts are paraphrased and one quotation is used. Neither the nomination's Lincoln/Humphreys account nor LighthouseFriends' has been checked against a primary contract. Fact-check 2026-10-22 (sentence-by-sentence against the nomination, LighthouseFriends, Thompson's letter as printed by AccessGenealogy and in the Richmond Palladium of 26 Nov 1836 (masthead confirmed through the newspapers tool: Richmond, Wayne County, Ind.), the USLHS record, Rowlett, VisitFlorida and Discover Florida Parks). Changed in the story: the rescue timing (per the letter, the Motto's boats came to the landing on the afternoon of the attack and the kite and twine rescue came the next morning; the letter's own dating, 'Monday, July 5', is wrong for 1836 and is not used); the walls sentence (the nomination says the destruction of the lighthouse uncovered the fraud, not 'after the 1836 fire' as a reported sequence); the 1837 $10,000 now footnoted to LighthouseFriends; the replica buildings are attributed to Rowlett and the USLHS record (1970), and LighthouseFriends' 1978 rebuilding is attributed separately; the 1855 lens is footnoted to LighthouseFriends; the inference 'so it is not a Coast Guard light' is removed; the tour days and step counts are now sourced and the step disagreement (95 at Discover Florida Parks, 109 at VisitFlorida) is stated. Record: the facts had the 1825 tower at 29 m; corrected to the 1846 tower (95 ft after 1855) with the 1825 tower at 65 ft (20 m). Open source conflicts: the USLHS record gives 'Height of light above mean high water, in feet: 75', against Rowlett's 95 ft (29 m) focal plane (the facts keep Rowlett's figure); lamps, 15 (LighthouseFriends) or 17 (USLHS), both given in the story.
